summary: A DigitalOcean Community tutorial by Pankaj explaining the difference between Java heap space and stack memory, using a simple sample program to trace how primitives, object references and objects are placed in each during execution. It concludes with a list of eight differences covering access scope, memory management, lifetime, JVM options, error types and speed. The page's navigation, comments and marketing boilerplate are ignored.
one_line: Pankaj's DigitalOcean tutorial explaining Java heap versus stack memory allocation, with a worked example and a list of key differences.
key_facts: The tutorial was published on August 3, 2022 and is authored by Pankaj.
Java heap space is used by the Java runtime to allocate memory to objects and JRE classes.
Garbage Collection runs on the heap memory to free memory used by objects that have no reference.
Java stack memory is used for the execution of a thread and is referenced in LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) order.
Whenever a method is invoked, a new block is created in the stack memory to hold local primitive values and references.
In the sample program, the string created in line 7 goes in the String Pool in the heap space, with a reference in the foo() stack block.
Heap memory is used by all parts of the application, whereas stack memory is used only by one thread of execution.
Stack memory only contains local primitive variables and reference variables to objects in heap space.
The JVM options -Xms and -Xmx define the startup and maximum size of heap memory, and -Xss defines the stack memory size.
When stack memory is full, Java runtime throws java.lang.StackOverFlowError.
When heap memory is full, Java runtime throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java Heap Space.
Stack memory is very fast compared to heap memory because of the simplicity of LIFO allocation.
Heap memory is divided into Young-Generation and Old-Generation, among others.
